blocks.content: Glacial erosion transforms pre-existing river V-shaped valleys into broad, steep-sided U-shaped troughs through plucking and abrasion.

rows: Lifting away of jointed blocks of rock frozen into moving ice
Scouring, scratching, and polishing of bedrock by rock fragments embedded in ice
Jointed or fractured bedrock and freeze-thaw meltwater activity
Presence of hard debris and rock fragments carried along glacier base
Jagged, rough, and uneven rock faces
Striated, polished, and grooved rock surfaces

items: Distinguish Erosional vs Depositional Landforms: Cirques, Horns, Arêtes, Fiords, and Roche Moutonnées are purely EROSIONAL landforms, whereas Moraines, Drumlins, Eskers, and Kames are DEPOSITIONAL.
Roche Moutonnée Features: Frequently asked in Prelims—the smooth, gently sloping up-glacier (stoss) side is formed by abrasion, while the steep, rugged down-glacier (lee) side is formed by plucking.
Valley Profiles: Fluvial valleys are V-shaped with interlocking spurs, whereas Glacial valleys are U-shaped with truncated spurs.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Glacial erosion proceeds mainly through two distinct physical mechanisms: plucking (lifting of fractured bedrock blocks) and abrasion (striating and polishing by embedded sediment load).
Cirques (or corries) are arm-chair-shaped, steep-walled depressions carved at glacier sources that often contain cirque lakes or tarns upon melting.
Headward erosion of multiple adjacent cirques creates sharp, knife-edge ridges called arêtes and pyramidal peaks termed horns.
Glaciers transform narrow, V-shaped river valleys into broad, flat-bottomed U-shaped glacial troughs.
Hanging valleys are tributary valleys truncated high above the main valley floor, creating spectacular waterfalls after glacial retreat.
